title: How Much You Need to Retire at 67 (Full Social Security Age)
description: The standard retirement path: Benchmarks, Social Security, and Medicare.
content:
Age 67 is the 'Full Retirement Age' (FRA) for most Americans born after 1960. Retiring at this age aligns perfectly with maximum Social Security benefits (100% payout) and Medicare eligibility (which starts at 65). Because your timeline is longer and your government benefits are fully activated, the savings requirement for retiring at 67 is significantly lower than retiring at 50 or 55. This guide explains the 'Standard Path' to a secure retirement.

Key Takeaways

  • The 10x Salary Rule: Fidelity recommends having 10 times your final annual salary saved by age 67. If you earn $80,000, aim for $800,000.
  • Social Security as the Floor: At 67, Social Security replaces ~40% of the average earner's income. Your portfolio only needs to generate the remaining 40-60% to maintain your lifestyle.
  • Medicare Safety: Since you are over 65, you don't need to budget for expensive private health insurance. You just need to cover Medicare Part B/D premiums and supplements.
  • Shorter Duration: A portfolio at 67 only needs to last ~20-25 years (to age 90). This allows for a slightly higher Safe Withdrawal Rate (4.5% or 5%) compared to early retirees.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Most Americans retire before 67, often involuntarily due to health or layoffs. Aiming for 67 is a solid plan, but having enough savings to flex to 65 if needed is a smart hedge.

The Math of Age 67

Scenario: Household spending $60,000/year.

1. Income Sources

Social Security (at FRA): $2,500/month ($30,000/year).
The Gap: $60,000 - $30,000 = $30,000/year needed.

2. Portfolio Requirement

Using the 4% Rule: $30,000 / 0.04 = $750,000.
Note: This is much lower than the $1.5M needed for early retirees because Social Security does the heavy lifting.

3. Savings Rate Needed

To hit $750,000 by age 67:
- Start at 25: Save $250/mo.
- Start at 35: Save $550/mo.
- Start at 45: Save $1,300/mo.
Verdict: Retiring at 67 is highly achievable for almost anyone who saves consistently.

The 'Catch Up' Phase (Age 50-67)

  1. Catch-Up Contributions: From age 50 to 67, you can put extra money in 401(k)s ($30,500 limit) and IRAs. This 'Sprint' phase can make up for a slow start in your 20s.
  2. Debt Freedom: The goal is to enter age 67 with a paid-off mortgage. Eliminating your largest bill reduces your 'Required Income', making your portfolio go further.
  3. Asset Allocation Shift: By 67, you should likely be 50% Stocks / 50% Bonds. You switch from 'Wealth Accumulation' to 'Wealth Preservation'.
  4. Delay to 70? If you are healthy and enjoy work, waiting until 70 to claim Social Security increases your check by another 24%. It is the best 'guaranteed return' available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I still need stocks?

Yes. At 67, you might live to 97. You need stocks to protect against 30 years of inflation. Going 100% cash/bonds ensures your purchasing power will die before you do.

What about Long Term Care?

This is the biggest risk. Medicare doesn't cover nursing homes. Ideally, reserve a portion of your home equity or portfolio specifically for end-of-life care.

Is my 401(k) taxed?

Yes. Withdrawals are taxed as Ordinary Income. Plan for this tax bill. Your $30k withdrawal might only net you $25k spendable cash.
